Consult Summary:
48-year-old man with 3-day history of watery diarrhoea, central abdominal pain and one episode of vomiting; likely self-limiting infectious gastroenteritis. Background of asthma treated with an inhaler, family history of bowel cancer.

Problem List:

Issue 1: Acute diarrhoea with abdominal pain and vomiting (3 days)
- Watery stools every few minutes; urges persist after each motion.
- Central, peri-umbilical abdominal pain, mildly tender on self-palpation; partly relieved after bowel motion; no radiation.
- One episode of vomiting this morning after eating fruit; no blood.
- No haematochesia or melena.
- No documented fever (patient unsure, reports mild sweating); no chest pain; walking/talking unchanged.
- Likely infectious gastroenteritis (food-borne). Differential: inflammatory bowel disease flare, irritable bowel syndrome, but less likely given acute onset and vomiting.

Issue 2: Asthma (chronic)
- Baseline shortness of breath controlled with inhaler; no increased respiratory symptoms reported.
- New inhaler brand started recently; patient doubts link to current GI symptoms.

Issue 3: Anxiety regarding family history of bowel cancer
- Father died of bowel cancer 10 years ago; patient concerned current symptoms could indicate malignancy.

Medications:
- Inhaler for asthma (brand and dose/route/frequency not documented).

Allergies:
- NKDA (No Known Drug Allergies).

Past Medical History:
- Asthma.

Social History:
- Currently off work due to frequent bowel motions; other social factors (smoking, alcohol, living arrangements) not documented.

Preventative History:
- No information on colorectal screening, vaccines, or other preventive measures documented.

Physical Examination:
- Remote consultation; vitals not obtained.
- Patient‐reported findings: mild central abdominal tenderness on palpation; no visible blood in stool or vomitus.

Plan:
- Oral rehydration: encourage liberal fluid intake (water, oral rehydration solutions).
- Diet: small, bland meals as tolerated; avoid dairy, caffeine, alcohol until settled.
- Red flag monitoring: seek in-person GP review if fever develops, blood in stool/vomit, worsening abdominal pain, signs of dehydration, or symptoms persist beyond 1–2 days.
- No antibiotics at present; likely viral/bacterial gastroenteritis that is self-limiting.
- Stay home from work until symptoms improve to reduce spread.
- Arrange GP follow-up for reassessment and to discuss appropriate colorectal cancer screening given family history.

Quality checks (document_quality):

● Missing but expected: objective vitals (temperature, pulse, BP), full medication list with doses, complete allergy verification, smoking/alcohol history, recent vaccinations/screening history.
● Internal conflicts: DOB initially quoted as 1992 then corrected; age clarified as 48 (conflict resolved).
● Transcript quality: clear overall; minor background noise and repetitions but clinically adequate.
